title: The Best Thanksgiving Menu Is a Southern Buffet
summary: Seconds are encouraged at Eric Kim’s Korean American dinner and love letter to the South.
body_markdown:
Seconds are encouraged at Eric Kim’s Korean American dinner and love letter to the South.


By[Eric Kim](https://cooking.nytimes.com/author/eric-kim)


Published Nov. 9, 2026


Updated Nov. 9, 2026


The Philadelphia chef Amanda Shulman once showed me, after a meal at her restaurant[Her Place](https://www.herplacephilly.com/) , a scrapbook filled with menus of every dinner party she’d cooked at home. What a great way to honor not just the meals prepared but the memories created and time well shared, I thought.


I was entering a new stage of life and wanted to live more intentionally, earnestly, to show love to the people who most matter to me. So, at the start of this year, inspired by Ms. Shulman, I vowed to have more friends over for dinner.


If love is attention, then cooking must be its purest manifestation. Cooking is how I thank people and tell them how much I care. A tablecloth, a lit candle and a generous spread can say so much more than a handwritten letter.


I suppose, then, what follows — my[Thanksgiving](https://cooking.nytimes.com/topics/thanksgiving) table — is an extension of that, a reflection of how I cook for those I love, and of my background, tastes and predilections.


I’m a Southern boy at heart, having grown up in Atlanta with casseroles and country-style buffets after church on Sundays. But my family roots are in South Korea, where jangs like gochujang, doenjang and soy sauce aren’t just culinary parlor tricks; they’re foundational.


A brown gravy, for instance, can gain immeasurable savoriness from a dollop of doenjang. If gochujang makes its way into the[cranberry sauce](https://cooking.nytimes.com/recipes/1018928-cranberry-sauce?art=100000011240079) , then so be it. I serve it all informally, in a love letter to the Southern buffet, where you want an eclectic mix of dishes that work together.


Credit...


Jonathan Bang


Some of these 10 recipes are more involved than others, but all are easy and will, I hope, teach you something new and inspire you to stretch a bit: to tackle a cooking project, perfect a culinary technique, maybe even dive into your first solo roast turkey.


I like to spread the work across three days. On the first day, I do the grocery shopping, start thawing the turkey, chop all the vegetables and make the pickles. On the second, I dry-brine the turkey and prepare the casseroles just before the point of baking, covering and refrigerating them. On the feast day itself, I roast the turkey, bake off the casseroles and prepare the fresh vegetable sides.


With this meal, I have just one rule: Everyone makes their own plate. I like to pile mine high, everything smothered in brown gravy, with room for seconds, thirds and pudding. My husband is partial to the squash macaroni and cheese, but the unanimous favorite among my friends seems to be the kale and cheese rice casserole. My hope is that you’ll find a new favorite in this collection, cook it for those you love and remember what matters most: standing side-by-side, catching up between sips of wine, working together toward a meal, like a last supper at the end of the world.

## The Recipes


---


## [Quick-Pickled Radishes, Cauliflower and Cucumbers](https://cooking.nytimes.com/recipes/793197871-quick-pickled-radishes-cauliflower-and-cucumbers?art=100000011240079)


Credit...


Armando Rafael for The New York Times. Food Stylist: Barrett Washburne. Prop Stylist: Paige Hicks.


Drawing on quick-pickling methods from South Korea and the American South, this recipe makes three distinctly flavored and irresistibly crunchy pickles. For a proper Southern relish tray, set them out with crackers, olives and cheese, and enjoy with[cocktails](https://cooking.nytimes.com/68861692-nyt-cooking/1834595-thanksgiving-cocktail-and-drink-recipes) or the rest of the meal. (Don’t forget to tuck leftovers into turkey sandwiches.)


Recipe: **[Quick-Pickled Radishes, Cauliflower and Cucumbers](https://cooking.nytimes.com/recipes/793197871-quick-pickled-radishes-cauliflower-and-cucumbers?art=100000011240079)**


---


## [Roast Turkey With Garlic and Chiles](https://cooking.nytimes.com/recipes/793198657-roast-turkey-with-garlic-and-chiles?art=100000011240079)


Credit...


Credit...


Roasting a whole buttered turkey alongside heads of garlic, dried chiles and tomato leaves you with a fantastic base for a[Thanksgiving dinner](https://cooking.nytimes.com/article/thanksgiving-recipes-staff-picks) . Those aromatics will not only infuse the pan juices that baste the turkey, but also tint it fire red. A dry brine is crucial here — most good turkey recipes call for this — as it seasons the meat through and through and helps it retain moisture even after a long roast.


Recipe: **[Roast Turkey With Garlic and Chiles](https://cooking.nytimes.com/recipes/793198657-roast-turkey-with-garlic-and-chiles?art=100000011240079)**


Advertisement


---


## [Doenjang Cream Gravy](https://cooking.nytimes.com/recipes/793199659-doenjang-cream-gravy?art=100000011240079)


Credit...


Credit...


A great gravy starts with flavorful drippings and a good stock. Here, doenjang, the Korean fermented soybean paste, lends both high and low notes, while a splash of cream at the end rounds it out. If you can’t find doenjang, then white or red miso works in a pinch. Additional gamchil mat (the Korean word for “savory taste”) comes in the form of Worcestershire sauce, though soy sauce tastes great as well.


Recipe: **[Doenjang Cream Gravy](https://cooking.nytimes.com/recipes/793199659-doenjang-cream-gravy?art=100000011240079)**


---


## [Scallion Smashed Potatoes](https://cooking.nytimes.com/recipes/793274360-scallion-smashed-potatoes?art=100000011240079)


Credit...


These smashed red potatoes might seem understated — tasting distinctively of, well,[potatoes](https://cooking.nytimes.com/article/thanksgiving-potato-recipes) — but they’re key to extending the richer flavors on the[Thanksgiving table](https://cooking.nytimes.com/article/thanksgiving-recipes-staff-picks) . A flurry of thinly sliced scallions adds welcome freshness, and a cream infused with dried shiitake mushrooms, nutmeg and those scallion whites helps match gravy’s super savory depth.


Recipe: **[Scallion Smashed Potatoes](https://cooking.nytimes.com/recipes/793274360-scallion-smashed-potatoes?art=100000011240079)**


---


## [Sausage and Apple Cornbread Stuffing](https://cooking.nytimes.com/recipes/793272490-sausage-and-apple-cornbread-dressing?art=100000011240079)


Credit...


Credit...


Armando Rafael for The New York Times. Food Stylist: Young Gun Lee. Prop Stylist: Paige Hicks.


Traditional Southern cornbread dressing is a tender union of everything delicious and good in the world, and in this modern spin on sausage stuffing, it’s crumbled along with saltine crackers to soak up broth like a sponge, keeping things moist, not wet. (It even coheres the stuffing’s disparate parts without the need for eggs.) Fennel seeds, fresh sage and dried red chile amplify the spiced, comforting notes, while sweet-tart apples, first marinated in cider vinegar to set the red color, punctuate the dish with acidity and sweetness.


Recipe: **[Sausage and Apple Cornbread Stuffing](https://cooking.nytimes.com/recipes/793272490-sausage-and-apple-cornbread-dressing?art=100000011240079)**


Advertisement

## [Kale and Cheese Rice Casserole](https://cooking.nytimes.com/recipes/793279219-kale-and-cheese-rice-casserole?art=100000011240079)


Credit...


Kale replaces broccoli in this rustic spin on a classic Southern casserole, adding some necessary roughage to your spread. Leafy Tuscan kale cooks down in a thin sauce of milk, onion and nutmeg, then mixes with plump rice and white Cheddar. A final grating of Parmesan on top becomes crisp and toasty in the oven.


Recipe: **[Kale and Cheese Rice Casserole](https://cooking.nytimes.com/recipes/793279219-kale-and-cheese-rice-casserole?art=100000011240079)**


---


## [Acorn Squash Macaroni and Cheese](https://cooking.nytimes.com/recipes/793279567-acorn-squash-macaroni-and-cheese?art=100000011240079)


Credit...


Credit...


Sliced orange squash gives classic macaroni and cheese a golden glow. Four cheeses — cream cheese for creaminess, Cheddar for sharpness, smoked Gouda for intrigue and Pepper Jack for a little kick — work together here to create an elegant but deeply comforting flavor, texture and look. Enjoy this mac gooey and warm, fresh out of the oven, or wait until it cools completely to slice into clean squares that can be griddled back to temperature or baked until crisp at the edges.


Recipe: **[Acorn Squash Macaroni and Cheese](https://cooking.nytimes.com/recipes/793279567-acorn-squash-macaroni-and-cheese?art=100000011240079)**


---


## [Soy-Butter Glazed Green Beans and Carrots](https://cooking.nytimes.com/recipes/793279903-soy-butter-glazed-green-beans-and-carrots?art=100000011240079)


Credit...


A touch of soy adds oomph to stovetop vegetables, while a slick of butter leaves them looking glossy and vibrant. Be sure to cut your vegetables into small, narrow pieces so they cook evenly in the quick 10-minute burst of heat this recipe calls for. Roll-cutting the carrots is a great way to practice your knife skills.


Recipe: **[Soy-Butter Glazed Green Beans and Carrots](https://cooking.nytimes.com/recipes/793279903-soy-butter-glazed-green-beans-and-carrots?art=100000011240079)**


Advertisement


---


## [Gochujang Cranberry Sauce](https://cooking.nytimes.com/recipes/793280238-gochujang-cranberry-sauce?art=100000011240079)


Credit...


Canned cranberry jelly is a beautiful starting place for balancing bold Korean flavors. When melted down and mixed with gochujang, vinegar, soy sauce and garlic, the sauce becomes a savory, tangy accent on a[Thanksgiving](https://cooking.nytimes.com/topics/thanksgiving) plate, uplifting roast turkey and even playing well with mashed potatoes. A smear of this is fantastic in a leftover turkey sandwich.


Recipe: **[Gochujang Cranberry Sauce](https://cooking.nytimes.com/recipes/793280238-gochujang-cranberry-sauce?art=100000011240079)**


---


## [Cardamom Banana Pudding](https://cooking.nytimes.com/recipes/793280484-big-bowl-of-cardamom-banana-pudding?art=100000011240079)


Credit...


Instead of pie, a fluffy banana pudding scented with cardamom is light enough to linger over after a big feast. Make this the day before (and at least the night before) serving, so the vanilla wafers can absorb the cream and become soft and silky.


Recipe: **[Cardamom Banana Pudding](https://cooking.nytimes.com/recipes/793280484-big-bowl-of-cardamom-banana-pudding?art=100000011240079)**
